title: Installing QGIS
text:
QGIS Version
Throughout this course, one of the software that we will be using is QGIS. Compared to ArcGIS Pro, which is a proprietary commercial software requiring (expensive) annual subscriptions, QGIS is free and open-source. ArcGIS Pro natively runs on Windows; QGIS runs on Windows, macOS, and Linux. Although QGIS might not be as polished and intuitive as ArcGIS Pro, the skills you build here will make it very easy to switch to ArcGIS Pro later, if needed.
We will be using the Long Term Release (LTR) of the software, specifically 3.44. This version will support a vast library of Python plugins that we may need in this course. QGIS 4.x may experience plugin incompatibilities and still require developers to update some of the tools.

title: Installing QGIS
text:
Download QGIS
Use this link (https://www.qgis.org/download/) to download QGIS. Select your operating system from the drop-down list.



Selecting platform for QGIS


For Windows users, follow the steps in the installer to install QGIS. For macOS, drag app packages into your Applications folder.






Important



Please make sure that you are using QGIS LTR 3.44 for this course.

title: Installing Metashape
text:
Version
On this page, you will be guided to install Metashape, one of the leading photograpmmetric processing software. First, download their installer based on your OS: https://www.agisoft.com/downloads/installer/. Run the installer as administrator; you may need to enter your OS login credentials.
Please note that we will be using Agisoft Metashape 2.3.2 Professional Edition.

title: Installing Metashape
text:
Activation
For now, we will be using a free 30-day trial. Open Metashape and select Start a free 30-day trial in the pop-up Activation window. Depending on your OS, you may need to enter your log-in credentials again.



Free 30-day trial in Metashape








Note



Please note that the interface/nomenclature may look different depending on your OS. The screenshots in this tutorial were captured using macOS.

title: CORONA and HEXAGON Imagery
text:
Background and Objectives
In this lab we will learn how to find and use declassified CORONA and HEXAGON satellite imagery. We will learn some basic tools for using raster and vector data in a GIS framework and will explore the ways in which archaeological features appear on historical imagery. We will then attempt to identify sites in a region of eastern Syria.
This first page will guide you to acquire a corrected CORONA image.
crumbs: Lab 1 Historical Satellite Imagery and GIS Basics

Files for this lab
For this lab, you will need to download the following files. Please make sure to log in using your Dartmouth credentials before downloading.

title: CORONA and HEXAGON Imagery
text:
Acquiring Raw Imagery (Optional)
CORONA images can be searched and downloaded or purchased from the USGS through their EarthExplorer site: http://earthexplorer.usgs.gov/. If you want to see all the available CORONA images, you can find them under Data Sets -> Declassified Data -> Declass 1 (1996). HEXAGON images can be found under Declass 3 (2013).



USGS EarthExplorer


By checking the Stereo High option under Additional Criteria -> Camera Resolution, you can search for only the latest generation KH-4B CORONA imagery, by checking Stereo Medium you can see KH-4A imagery. Note however that none of this imagery has been orthorectified. It is highly distorted and cannot be used for mapping purposes. By selecting a single point in your area of interest in the Search Criteria tab, EarthExplorer will return all possible images that cover the point.






Tip



How to choose the best image? For each image, use the footprint tool to see the approximate area covered by each frame. You can also press the Show Metadata and Browse icon under each image to see image details. Pay close attention to the acquisition date.



EarthExplorer Tools





CORONA and HEXAGON Nomenclature
All CORONA images have a unique entity ID number that looks like this: DS 1102-1025D A042. These numbers can be parsed as follows:

Similarly, an entity ID for HEXAGON images, such as D3C 1219-300919 A026, can be decoded as such:

title: CORONA and HEXAGON Imagery
text:
Getting Orthorectified Images
CORONA and HEXAGON satellites used a cross-path panoramic camera that produced elongated film strips. The imaging geometry of the camera and the surface of the earth result in a “bow tie” area of the ground being compressed into the rectangular area of the film. Further, the image motion compensators built into the imaging system did not fully account for the satellites motion during the image scan, which creates an “S” shaped pattern of distortion from one side of the image to the other. A third source of image distortion is derived from the topography of the ground as the parallax changes between the ground and the imaging surface inside the camera. These characteristics result in severe spatial distortions that radically alter the shape and size of individual features, in opposite directions on forward and aft cameras.



Spatial distortions of the CORONA images








Note



Tools such as SUNSPOT allow you to correct these distortions by selecting multiple ground-control points against contemporary satellite imagery.



CORONA Atlas
For this lab, we will use previously orthorectified CORONA images from the CORONA Atlas Project (http://corona.cast.uark.edu/index.html).
Open the link above and explore the Atlas. Areas with available CORONA imagery are shown outlined in red, and mission numbers indicated (if you zoom in), overlaid on modern Google Maps data:
In the drop-down Map Contents window, sites and mission numbers can be toggled on and off. Drop down the CORONA tab to reveal mission numbers and dates of imagery available in the display window.






Tip



Slider bars appearing to the right of each image series can be used to fade on or off individual missions, or all CORONA simultaneously to facilitate comparison with modern imagery. At the bottom of the screen there is also a swipe tool to reveal modern imagery on the right and CORONA on the left.





Map Contents window in CORONA Atlas


Using the Tools Menu The tools menu offers several important functions. You can enter coordinates in Lat/Long (decimal degrees) to zoom to a particular location. You may also change the basemap to several different options. The Atlas also offers a basic archaeological site database for certain regions of the world, to aid as a navigational guide for archaeological research. At the bottom of the tools menu there are several measurement and mapping tools, enabling you to measure distance, area and points.



Tools in CORONA Atlas








ImportantEXERCISE 1



In CORONA Atlas, locate the archaeological site of Tell Beidar (Beydar) in Syria (40.5872, 36.7382), a large Early Bronze Age (3000-2000 BC) site. Using Area Measurement Tool, measure the area within the outer wall. Report the area in your lab response.








ImportantEXERCISE 2



At least three different CORONA missions are available for the Tell Beidar area. Use the Map Contents tool to turn on and off different options. Which missions and cameras do you think are best for archaeological visibility? Why?




Download CORONA imagery from the Atlas
In order to download imagery from the CORONA Atlas, go to the Map Contents menu, drop down the CORONA imagery tab, and then drop down the Mission/Revolution series. Simply push the download button to the right of an individual frame to begin the download.
For this lab, we will be using the CORONA image 1105-1025F057, which covers the Tell Beidar area. Download it from the Map Contents window. You will be given a prompt to select a download for either a GeoTIFF image or an NITF — select GeoTIFF.






Note



You can also use this link to download the image: https://drive.google.com/file/d/14eqZTAxHDJDMNHID_UMSVgaNf0vhYwiu/view?usp=drive_link






Casana, Jesse, David D. Goodman, and Carolin Ferwerda. 2023. “A Wall or a Road? A Remote Sensing-Based Investigation of Fortifications on Rome’s Eastern Frontier.” Antiquity 97 (396): 1516–33. https://doi.org/10.15184/aqy.2023.153.
crumbs: Lab 1 Historical Satellite Imagery and GIS Basics

title: Rasters
text:
Background
The central power of GIS is in the ability to load multiple spatial datasets into a single map frame, and then compare them to one another, either visually or quantitatively. Raster graphics are grids of pixels, such as CORONA imagery, scanned maps, and elevation models. Vectors are composed of discrete data points, such as points, lines, and polygons, which include archaeological sites, rivers, and soil types. Rasters are usually larger files and require more computing power to process.
This page will guide you to load a Bing basemap and three rasters into a new project in QGIS.
crumbs: Lab 1 Historical Satellite Imagery and GIS Basics

title: Rasters
text:
Basemaps
In QGIS, basemaps are background reference layers, such as the satellite imagery in CORONA Atlas. They are usually raster images streamed from an online server, so you can view them but not edit them. Basemaps provide visual context rather than data for direct spatial analysis.
Start a new project in QGIS using Project -> New and save it in a folder for ANTHRO_50_03_LAB1. Because of the highly iterative nature of GIS work, give your project a specific and descriptive name: e.g., DA2609_Lab1_YourName_1. Start your filename with a letter and not a number.



Start a new project in QGIS








Tip



Make sure to save your project regularly by pressing Ctrl/CMD + s or the button  near the top. Alternatively, use an autosave plugin.


You will notice that the map view is currently blank, which makes it hard to navigate. We need to add a basemap. Locate the “Browser” panel on the left side of the screen.



Browser panel in QGIS


Right-click on XYZ Tiles and select New Connection. Type a name for the layer, such as Bing Satellite. Paste the following into the URL field and click OK: http://ecn.t3.tiles.virtualearth.net/tiles/a{q}.jpeg?g=1.
Double click on the XYZ Tiles Connection you just created, and you should be able to see the basemap loaded.



Bing Maps loaded in QGIS








Caution



Make sure the coordinate reference system (CRS) in the right bottom corner is set to EPSG:3857 for now, used for display by many web-based mapping tools. This is a projected coordinate system that flattens the curved surface of the Earth (as opposed to a geographic coordinate system), and should not be used for rigorous analysis.
crumbs: Lab 1 Historical Satellite Imagery and GIS Basics

title: Rasters
text:
Adding Raster Layers

CORONA ds1105-1025df057.tif
To add a raster in QGIS, select Layer -> Add Layer -> Add Raster Layer.



Adding a raster in QGIS


In the Data Source Manager, under Source, locate ds1105-1025df057.tif stored in your computer and click Add.



QGIS — Data Source Manager (directory may be different in your computer)


Return to the map view. In the Layers window, right-click on the raster layer we just added and select Zoom to Layer(s). Wait for a few moments for the image to load.



Right-click on a raster layer








Caution



Files are linked to a GIS — not stored — and any moved files must be re-linked in QGIS.


In the Layers window, toggle off the raster layer to see the underlying satellite imagery. Toggle it on again. In the coordinate near the bottom of the interface, type in 4518140.3,4402634.6 to find Tell Beydar again. In scale, type in 1:5000 (1 cm on the screen represents 5,000 cm on the ground).






ImportantEXERCISE 3



Toggle on and off the CORONA image, look for changes evident in the close vicinity of Tell Beydar. Please describe these changes and what you think may have caused them. Be sure to describe their location relative to the Tell.




Survey Map from Tony Wilkinson (2002)
Download Lab1Wilkinson.zip and unzip it in your computer. Add a raster layer that links to Wilkinson_2002.tif. This map was produced by an archaeologist, Tony Wilkinson, who did an archaeological survey in the area around Tell Beydar. The map has already been georeferenced, meaning that it has been transformed to match the other geographical data.
The imported map may look funny in QGIS. This is because the raster only contains pixels with two values, 0 and 255, and the program automatically assigns a color to each of these two colors.
To correct this, right-click on Wilkinson_2002 layer, select Symbology, and change Render type to Singleband gray.



Change layer symbology in QGIS


While you are at it, locate Transparency tab on the right side of the layer properties window, adjust the opacity of this layer to 50%.



Change layer opacity in QGIS




1938 Historical Map
Now it is time to put what you learned about rasters to practice! Download 1938_FrenchMap.zip and unzip it. Add 1014562_LVT2_Hassetche_NJ_37_XI_partie_sud_NJ_37_V_1938.TIF as a raster layer. Change the layer’s opacity to 60%. Toggle off layer Wilkinson_2002.
While the map has been similarly georeferenced, the georeferencing is not perfect for this historical map.



The 1938 historical map is not perfectly georeferenced


In QGIS, you can also measure distance and area in the map view. To do so, use the Measure Line tool in the top toolbar and click on the points in the map view.



Measure toolbar in QGIS








ImportantEXERCISE 4



With both the CORONA image and the 1938 map toggled visible in the Layers panel, measure the georeferencing error of the 1938 map. To do so, first measure and report the distance in meters between the center of Tell Beydar on the CORONA image and its center on the map. Recall that the CORONA image has a spatial resolution of about 2 meters per pixel here. Report error/offset between the map and the CORONA image in CORONA pixels.
Now look at the western and eastern ends of the ribbon-shaped corrected CORONA image. Compared with the area around Tell Beydar, is the level of detail there finer, coarser, or about the same? Why?
crumbs: Lab 1 Historical Satellite Imagery and GIS Basics

title: Vectors
text:
Background
Vector data are discrete points, lines, and polygons, and often have tables attached to them containing ancillary information. The most common file type for storing vector data in QGIS is a “shapefile” (.shp).
crumbs: Lab 1 Historical Satellite Imagery and GIS Basics

title: Vectors
text:
Adding Vectors
Download a shapefile of all archaeological sites in this region: Lab1_AllSites.zip. Similar to adding rasters, navigate to Layer -> Add Layer -> Add Vector Layer.... In the window, select AllSites.shp under Source and add to the map.
Right-click on the newly added vector layer and select Zoom to Layer(s) to see its full extent.
Zoom to Layer(s) allows you to see the full extent of a vector layer, but sometimes an outlier can unduly affect the map view. In this case, there seems to be a data point in an unlikely place in the southern end of the map view.



Zoom to all sites in QGIS


Use the Identify Features  in the top toolbar and click on this outlier to examine it.






ImportantEXERCISE 5



Find the point that lies far from the rest of the dataset. Using the Identify Results panel, report its name, latitude, and longitude. Do you think this point was there by design, or is it an error? If it is an error, what value is likely to be wrong?
crumbs: Lab 1 Historical Satellite Imagery and GIS Basics

title: Vectors
text:
Vector Attributes
For now, let us focus on the region near Tell Beydar. Toggle on only three layers: AllSites, ds1105-1025df057, and the basemap. Zoom to ds1105-1025df057. Examine the general distribution of these sites and answer the following question:






ImportantEXERCISE 6



Are there any patterns in the general distribution of all archaeological sites vis-à-vis geographical features such as water and topography?


Sometimes, we want to examine archaeological features of a particular type. To do that, right-click on AllSites and select Open Attribute Table.
In the Attribute Table, you can see each data point has some values or “attributes” associate with it. In the table, locate the column/field Type, which contains string/text values such as Mound, Other, Flat.



Attribute table in QGIS


To select all features that are of the mound type, click on Select by Expression tool () in the top toolbar. In the expression window, type in the following expression and press Select Features.
"Type" = 'Mound'
Close the Select by Expression window. Now, all the features that contain a Type value of Mound should be highlighted in the attributes table.
With the attributes table open, go back to the map view and right-click on the vector layer. Select Export -> Save Selected Features As...



Export selected data


In the window, select Esri Shapefile as the Format and use the ... button next to File name to save it in your computer with a name such as Lab1_mounds_2609.shp. Change the CRS to Project CRS. Click OK.



Exportation in QGIS


The new selected dataset should be added to your map. Toggle off the original vector layer, and you should be able to see all mounded sites in the region.



Mound features in the region








ImportantEXERCISE 7



Examine the attribute tables of both vector layers, how many features are there in each dataset? What is the percentage of mounds among all sites? As a bonus question, what is the percentage of the mounded site surveyed by a trustworthy surveyor such as Tuna?
crumbs: Lab 1 Historical Satellite Imagery and GIS Basics

text:
Image Analysis

title: Drone Photogrammetry
text:
Background Objectives
The rapidly growing sophistication of small, commercial drones or “UAVs” (unpiloted aerial vehicles) combined with the increasing power of digital photogrammetry software to produce 3D models and orthoimagery has begun to transform archaeological documentation and discovery. While just a few years ago, collecting low altitude aerial imagery was costly, cumbersome, and often dangerous, today it can be done reliably, quickly, and at low cost. Moreover, a growing range of small, lightweight cameras and sensors open new possibilities not only to map sites and landscapes, but to discover new sites and features that would otherwise be invisible.
In this lab, we will learn to process a series of drone-acquired images to produce high-resolution orthoimagery and a digital elevation model (DEM) of an archaeological site called Echo Canyon (Echo Mesa), located on the Hopi Reservation in Arizona. Collaborating with the Hopi Cultural Preservation Office, our team from the Spatial Archaeometry Lab (SPARCL) at Dartmouth has been undertaking drone-based surveys of numerous sites in order to assist with management and locate potentially unrecorded archaeological features.
Archaeologists Greg Schachner (UCLA) and Wes Bernardini (University of Redlands) previously did a systematic surface survey of Echo Canyon and recorded many archaeological features, including stone building foundations, circular storage pits, and refuse middens replete with artifacts. Our job is to see if we can locate any of these features and potentially find unrecorded features using drone imagery.
For this lab, we will be processing color drone images collected with a DJI M300 Enterprise drone, equipped with a 20MP visible light camera and a high-accuracy RTK GNSS (GPS). You will use a subset of these photos to create an orthoimage and a DEM of an area where archaeologists have previously recorded surface artifact scatters and potential building remains. We will then open these data in QGIS and compare them with a thermal image mosaic of the same site, publicly available color imagery, and observations of archaeological features that were mapped by our colleagues.

title: Drone Photogrammetry
text:
NoteOrthoimagery



An “orthophoto” is a photograph that has had all spatial distortions, caused by both camera parallax and ground topography, corrected such that it can be used as a map. If we process a bunch of photos together to produce a larger mosaic, then we have made an “ortho-image.”






Aerial view of Echo Canyon, Hopi Reservation, AZ

title: Drone Photogrammetry
text:
File Download
For this lab, you will need to download the following files.

Raw_Color_Photos: A folder that contains 34 color photos shot by the drone. You may need to unzip the file.
echocanyon_thermal_8may25_utm.tif: A thermal mosaic of the study region.
EchoMesa_GroundSurvey.gpkg: A geopackage that contains multiple vector datasets of archaeological features previously mapped.

title: Drone Photogrammetry
text:
Metashape Setup
For this lab, we will be using Agisoft Metashape. Follow the instruction on this page to install the software.
After activating the software, start a new file (File -> New) and save the project with a descriptive name such as DigitalArch_EchoMesa_Your_Name in a folder with the other files that you have just downloaded.


Add Photos
To add photos to make a 3D model, right-click on Chunk 1 in the Workspace, select Add -> Add Photos..., choose all 34 photos from Raw_Color_Photos, and click the Open button.



Adding photos to Metashape


Because these photos already have GPS points, Metashape will be able to position them correctly. Toggle Show Cameras  to see these locations.

title: Drone Photogrammetry
text:
Align Photos
At this stage we want to refine the camera position for each photo and builds a sparse point cloud. Select Align Photos command from the Workflow menu.
Set the following values for the parameters in the Align Photos dialogue:

Accuracy: High (lower accuracy settings can be used to get the rough camera positions in the shorter time)
Generic preselection and Reference preselection should be checked.




Aligning photos in Metashape


Click OK button to start photo alignment. This may take a while, but will align the photos and produce a point cloud in which you can see some of the features from the scene, as below:



Photos aligned in Metashape


The Move Region  tool is used to define the area you hope to map and can be used to eliminate extraneous datapoints. It is resizable and rotatable. Adjust it to a position you think looks good. Make it approximately the same size as the sparse point cloud you generated.






Tip



Use the mouse scroll or holding option/alt to pan the view.

title: Drone Photogrammetry
text:
Photogrammetry

Build Point Cloud/Dense Cloud
Based on the estimated camera positions, Metashape now creates a single dense point cloud. Select Build Point Cloud command from the Workflowmenu.
Set the following recommended values for the parameters in the Build Dense Cloud window:

Quality: Low (higher quality takes quite a long time and demands more computational resources)
Depth filtering: Mild (if the geometry of the scene to be reconstructed is complex with numerous small details on the foreground, then it is recommended to set Mild depth filtering mode, for important features not to be sorted out)

Click OK button to start building dense point cloud. When finished, be sure to turn on the Point Cloud option  at the top, and turn off Show Cameras to see the results better.



Build point cloud in Metashape




Build a Model/Mesh
After the dense point cloud has been reconstructed it is possible to generate a high-quality polygonal mesh model based on the dense cloud data, basically filling in areas between points in the point cloud to create a continuous surface. Select Build Model command from the Workflow menu.
Set the following recommended values for the parameters in the Build Mesh dialog:

Source data: Point cloud
Surface type: Height field (2.5D)
Face count: Medium (for faster processing)

Click OK button to start mesh reconstruction and ignore the warning.
You can now turn on the Model - Solid option () in the toolbar. Notice the areas in the mesh that look better and worse compared to the point cloud.


Build Texture
Next we will use the original photographs to map details (“texture”) onto the 3D model we are creating.  This will make it look a lot better but does not actually improve the underlying model.
Select Build Texture command from the Workflow menu. Use the following values for the Build Texture dialog:



Building texture in Metashape


Click OK button to start texture generation. This process may take a while. When it is done, turn on the textured model using the pyramid-shaped icon on the toolbar:



Show textured model in Metashape


Your model now should look approximately like this:



Textured model in Metashape




Build a DEM
Select Build DEM from the Workflow menu.  
Set the following recommended values for the parameters in the Build DEM window:

Projection: WGS 84 / UTM zone 12N (EPSG:32612)
Source data: Model/Mesh
Resolution: Default

After DEM generation, click File -> Export DEM.... Save the DEM with a descriptive name and select type TIFF/GeoTIFF. Check the Coordinate System is EPSG:32612.


Generate an Orthoimage
Select Build Orthomosaic… from the Workflow menu.
Set the following recommended values for the parameters in the Build Orthomosaic window and Click OK to start orthophoto generation.



Build Orthomosaic in Metashape


Finally, select File -> Export -> Export Orthomosaic... and select TIFF/GeoTIFF as the file type. Save your orthophoto with a descriptive name, such as DigitalArch_EchoMesa_Ortho_Date.






ImportantEXERCISE 1



Report, in that order, the following values in your Metashape project: number of tie points; number of Point Cloud points; spatial resolution of DEM; image size of the orthomosaic; and the file size of the orthomosaic.

title: Orthomosaic in QGIS
text:
Project Setup in QGIS
This page will guide you to analyze archaeological features in Echo Mesa using the orthomosaic you have just generated. Start QGIS and open a new project. Save it () in your Digital Archaeology Lab folder with a filename such as lab2_EchoMesa_Hopi_Your_LastName.qgz.
Change the CRS to EPSG:32612 to match that of the orthomosaic.
As before, from the Browser panel, drag a basemap such as Bing maps from XYZ Tiles to your Layers.
If any of the panels are not there, select View -> Panels to toggle them on.

title: Orthomosaic in QGIS
text:
Adding Data

Orthomosaic and DEM
In QGIS, add both the DEM and orthomosaic .tif files as raster layer. In the Layers panel, toggle off DEM and compare the resolution between the orthomosaic and the basemap.






ImportantEXERCISE 2



Compare our 2-cm-resolution drone image to the basemap. List, with screenshots or coordinates, at least three additional features that are only resolved in the orthomosaic.




Archaeological Features
Next, add EchoMesa_GroundSurvey.gpkg that you downloaded as a vector layer. When asked, select all items to add.



Adding .gpkg to QGIS


Next, convert these vectors to UTM zone 12N:



Converting coordinates between CRSs


In the Layers panel, select all four vector layers added, right-click on them, and choose Group Selected. Name the group as ground_survey_data. Now you can toggle on/off all archaeological features at once.



Grouping layers








ImportantEXERCISE 3



Based on the mapped archaeological features and Herrmann et al. (2018), discuss how ultra-high resolution orthoimagery and DEMs we produce using drones can help archaeologists discover, document, and interpret ancient sites and landscapes.




Thermal Imagery
Finally, add echocanyon_thermal_8may25_utm.tif as a raster layer. You may notice that the image looks rather “muted.”



Thermal image initially added to QGIS


To troubleshoot, we may need to examine the distribution of the pixel values. Right click on the thermal layer and select Properties. In Layer Properties window, go to Histogram and click Computer Histogram.






Note



For a single-band image such as this thermal image, a GIS program typically maps the range of pixel values onto a grayscale (0-255), from black for the lowest value to white for the highest.


As you can see here, the raster displays poorly because a few outlying values stretch this range. Most pixels fall within only about 10% of it, so they are squeezed into a narrow band of grays, and the variation within the histogram’s main peak is hard to see.



Thermal raster histogram





Thermal raster ideal histogram


To change this, go to Symbology dialog in Layer Properties. In the Min/Max Value Settings, select Cumulative count cut and choose 10 - 90%.



Changing layer symbology in QGIS


You should now have a much better visualization of the thermal data.



Thermal data overlaid by mapped features

title: Orthomosaic in QGIS
text:
Archaeology of Echo Mesa
A typical archaeological site in Echo Canyon consists of stone building foundations and artifact scatter at the surface:



A typical archaeological site in the study region


In QGIS map view, one similar site can be found near coordinates 570324.3092,3972901.0257. Locate this point and set the scale to 1:30.



Locating an archaeological site in Echo Mesa


Toggle off all layers except for the orthomosaic. Can you see the archaeological feature here?



An archaeological site in Echo Mesa


To map this feature, we will need to create a new vector layer. Go to Layer -> Create Layer -> New GeoPackage Layer.... In the pop-up window, first click ... next to the File name and select a location to save your layer with a reasonable name.
For Geometry type, select Polygon, and select Project CRS. In New Field, write ID in the Name field and change Type to Integer. Press Add to Fields List. Finally, press OK.





In the Layers panel, right-click on the newly created layer and select Toggle Editing (). This will let you edit the .gpkg file directly. In the top toolbars, select Add Polygon Feature () and start tracing the boundary of the archaeological site. Once done, hold Ctrl and click anywhere on the map. In the pop-up window, put 0 in the ID field, indicating this is the first site you map.



Adding new features to QGIS


There you go — you have just mapped your first archaeological feature in QGIS! It should look something like this:



Your first mapped archaeological site!


Once you are done, select Save Layer Edits () in the top toolbar. Click Toggle Editing () again to exit edit mode.






ImportantEXERCISE 4



Are you able to identify the archaeological feature you just mapped in the color orthoimage, DEM, or thermal mosaic of Echo Canyon? Was this feature previously mapped in EchoMesa_GroundSurvey?








ImportantEXERCISE 5



Are you able to recognize any other possible archaeological features? What data did you use to find these features? Please provide screenshots in your response, edit your newly created layer to include these features, and upload your .gpkg to Canvas. Make sure that the file name contains your name.








ImportantEXERCISE 6



Based on your work and our readings, including Materazzi and Pacifici (2022) and Paulsen et al. (2026), describe how thermal and near-infrared imagery are used by archaeologists to reveal features that are not visible otherwise.
